newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin tries to put Russia's house in order.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin tries to put Russia's house in order.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, trying to show he is strong enough after illness to put Russia's house in order, promoted his conservative interior minister to a higher cabinet rank on Tuesday to crack down on crime.

At meetings in the Kremlin with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and counter-intelligence chief Nikoilai Kovalyov, Yeltsin also took a firm stance on security issues and against NATO's eastward expansion plans.

In gestures which appeared designed to show he is firmly in charge, Yeltsin demanded action to protect Russia against a reported rise in foreign espionage and signalled to his defence minister and a top defence aide that they must stop bickering.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin had named Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov a deputy prime minister in charge of the tax police, customs service and other agencies dealing with economic crime.
"A need emerged for closer coordination...in the fight against crime, first of all economic crime," Yastrzhembsky said, adding that Kulikov will also remain interior minister.

Kulikov, 50, is the ninth deputy prime minister in the government. A career interior ministry soldier, he is widely considered the most conservative member of Chernomyrdin's cabinet and was an advocate of the use of force to smash separatist rebels in Chechnya.

But Kulikov, who has been interior minister since 1995, is not regarded as being as hawkish as some of his sacked predecessors such as former Yeltsin security chief Alexander Korzhakov and ousted defence minister Pavel Grachev.
Above all, he has been loyal to the president.
Yeltsin, still not back full-time in the Kremlin after 12 days treatment in hospital for pneumonia last month, is still under fire from political opponents who want him ousted for health reasons.

In a sign of the president's frailty, Chernomyrdin said in comments published by the Washington Post that he favoured holding Yeltsin's planned summit with President Bill Clinton next month in Europe rather than the United States.

The opposition communists say Yeltsin's heart problems, which have forced him to spend most of the last seven months out of the Kremlin, have put political, economic and military reforms on hold. Efforts to tackle crime, they say, have failed.
Yeltsin hit back with his meetings on Tuesday.

He reacted strongly when Federal Security Service (FSB) chief Kovalyov told him 11 foreign spies had been uncovered in the last six months and 32 Russians had been caught in the same period trying to hand over secret information.
"The president pointed to the need to improve the mechanisms for defending Russia's state interests," Yastrzhembsky said, but gave no others details.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had also told Defence Minister Igor Rodionov and Yuri Baturin, head of the separate Defence Council responsible for overseeing military reforms, to hold a joint news conference later this week.
The move was clearly intended to end rumours that the two men are at loggerheads over the path of reforms.

At his talks with Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin also touched on foreign policy before the prime minister leaves on Wednesday for talks in Washington. He reiterated opposition to NATO's plans to offer membership to some eastern and central European countries.
"Moscow's negative position on the proposed eastward expansion of NATO is very well known to our American partners," Yastrzhembsky said.

Yeltsin, Chernomyrdin and Kremlin chief of staff Anatoly Chubais have all condemned NATO's expansion plans in the last few days in a coordinated offensive warning the West that enlargement will strengthen Yeltsin's hardline opponents.
